clue.text: Trying places, maybe, for those involved with rackets

definitions.text: Trying places, maybe, for those involved with rackets

parts.words: Trying places, maybe, for those involved with rackets
parts.note: law courts where racketeers are tried read as tough venues, while tennis players with rackets use courts of a firm surface

explanation.surface: Courtrooms where those mixed up in criminal rackets face trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rackets' suggests crime and 'trying places' suggests courts of law; in fact these are tennis surfaces of asphalt or concrete, for players holding rackets.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is played on grass, clay or firm asphalt and concrete surfaces, the last being what racket players call this.

clue.text: William or Mary, for what it's worth

definitions.text: William or Mary, for what it's worth

parts.words: William or Mary, for what it's worth
parts.note: William III and Mary II reigned jointly, so each was one of a pair of monarchs; the phrase is also an old gold coin worth ten shillings

explanation.surface: A remark on the value of one of the joint monarchs William and Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: William and Mary shared the English throne, so each was half of the ruling pair; 'for what it's worth' points to the coin of that name, worth ten shillings in old British money.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint monarch holds one part of the crown, and the gold coin of that name was valued at ten shillings.

clue.text: Growth of Gibraltar originally?

parts.note: Gibraltar is nicknamed the Rock, so a plant growing there would be a growth of the Rock; the term really means an alpine grown in garden stones

explanation.surface: A question about what first grew on Gibraltar.
explanation.walkthrough: Gibraltar is commonly called 'the Rock', so a growth native to it suggests the gardener's term for alpines grown among stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpines and small perennials grown in rockeries are known by this gardening term.

clue.text: Character twice spotted in Panama

definitions.meaning: a punctuation mark made of two dots, one above the other
Colón is a port city at the Caribbean end of the Panama Canal

explanation.surface: Someone of note seen on two occasions in Panama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' seems to mean seen, but here it means bearing spots: the punctuation mark has two dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark made of two dots shares its spelling with Colón, a Panamanian port.

clue.text: Girl at the Hertfordshire town in the dark

parts.note: Una is a girl's name
Ware is a market town in Hertfordshire, a county north of London

explanation.surface: A young woman at a Hertfordshire town after nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: WARE is a small town in Hertfordshire, the English county just north of London. 'In the dark' means ignorant, not at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Being kept in the dark is an idiom for knowing nothing about something.

clue.text: Mathematicians called Steptoe, perhaps

definitions.meaning: people who tot up figures, that is add them
Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about rag-and-bone men, who collect scrap and are known in slang by this name

explanation.surface: Number-crunchers who go by the surname Steptoe.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about a father and son who were rag-and-bone men, scrap collectors known in slang as 'totters'; those who tot up sums are the other sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To tot is to add up figures, and also British slang for collecting scrap, as the Steptoes did.

clue.text: She's crazy about you, we hear

indicators.note: about means the word for crazy goes round the other piece

parts.note: crazy means mad

indicators.note: we hear means the word you is taken by its sound, a single letter

parts.note: you sounds like the letter U

explanation.surface: A woman who is mad about you, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy about you' looks like a lovesick phrase; MAD goes 'about' U, the letter that 'we hear' as 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Maud is a woman's name, so it can stand for a female referred to as she.

clue.text: Excuse for a party one joins

parts.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A reason given for going to a party that someone joins.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, used as an excuse for not having done something.

clue.text: How the nightwatchman kept himself amused off duty?

definitions.text: How the nightwatchman kept himself amused off duty?

parts.words: How the nightwatchman kept himself amused off duty?
parts.note: a night worker sleeps by day, so his dreams come in daylight; the word usually means drifting into reverie

explanation.surface: A question about a night guard's leisure hours.
explanation.walkthrough: A nightwatchman works nights, so when off duty he sleeps by day and his dreams happen in daytime.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantasising while awake is literally dreaming by daylight, which is what an off-duty night worker does.

clue.text: Left with sufficient strength can be easily moved

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
able means having enough power or strength

explanation.surface: Something left with enough strength to be shifted easily.
explanation.walkthrough: PORT is the nautical word for left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something carriable or movable without trouble is described as easy to carry about.

clue.text: Municipal body putting planner in his place?

definitions.meaning: a council running a town or district
an ... on a locality, or the council itself, that keeps a town planner in check

explanation.surface: A town council keeping its planning officer under control.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the words separately: a body with authority over the local area is the one able to put a planner in his place.
explanation.definitionFit: A council governing a town or county is the British term for such a municipal administration.

clue.text: See 10
Could nevertheless prove a close match

definitions.text: Could nevertheless prove a close match

parts.words: Could nevertheless prove a close match
parts.note: open seems the opposite of close, yet a game described as open can still be close in score

explanation.surface: A sporting contest that might still turn out tight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets 'open' against 'close' as opposites, though a free-flowing contest can still end with tied scores; in chess the term names openings begun with king's pawns.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-flowing contest with chances for both sides can still finish level, so open play and a close result coexist.

clue.text: One who sets his sights on reaching a German town

definitions.text: One who sets his sights on reaching
definitions.meaning: someone who makes an attempt or effort
An ancient city on the Moselle in Germany

explanation.surface: A traveller aiming to get to a town in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tries is the doer of an attempt, and the Moselle city of Roman origin carries the same spelling.

clue.text: See 1
By the sound of it look for a drink, but find a vegetable

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the phrase for looking for a drink is taken as heard

parts.note: to seek ale is to look for a drink

explanation.surface: Searching for a drink and ending up with greens instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seek ale' sounds the same as the name of a coastal vegetable related to cabbage.
explanation.definitionFit: This coastal brassica, a cabbage relative, has blanched shoots eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: They indict a couple of hundred employers

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two of them make CC
users are those who employ something

explanation.surface: Some two hundred bosses facing charges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employers' suggests bosses, but here it means people who employ, that is use, something.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who indict bring charges against someone, which is what plaintiffs and prosecutors do.

clue.text: Remote location from which Stalin henchman is heading back

indicators.note: heading back means the little word is points the other way

parts.note: Lavrentiy Beria was Stalin's secret police chief

explanation.surface: A far-off place to which one of Stalin's henchmen is returning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading back' turns IS into SI, which sits before BERIA, Stalin's feared secret police chief.
explanation.definitionFit: The vast Russian region was a byword for remoteness, the place of Soviet exile camps.

clue.text: Untidy Hugh's backdoor entry in dirty boots?

indicators.note: entry means the scrambled name is entered into the other piece

parts.note: door read backwards, back placed before it as the signal

indicators.note: untidy means the letters of the name are messed up

parts.note: the letters of Hugh's, with the s counted

explanation.surface: Hugh, a scruffy man, coming in by the back door in muddy boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backdoor' gives ROOD, door backwards; 'Untidy' scrambles HUGHS into UGHSH, and that 'entry' sits inside ROOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding over people with nailed horseshoes gave the phrase, so boots fitted for rough ground suit the question-marked definition.

clue.text: Virginia, I can't possibly see in Rome

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for the US state Virginia

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of the short phrase may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Someone named Virginia saying she cannot manage to sightsee in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a noun here, a bishop's seat: the Holy See. 'Possibly' rearranges ICANT into TICAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See, the Pope's seat of government, is in the Roman city-state of that name.

clue.text: Falls and gets up again with artist's help

indicators.note: gets up means the word again climbs, read backwards in a down entry

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps falling and getting back up with a painter's help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets up' reverses AGAIN to NIAGA in this down clue; RA, a Royal Academician, is the artist.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous waterfalls on the US-Canada border are known by this name.

clue.text: Introduction to a notable work

definitions.meaning: an opening piece or event leading into something
Wordsworth's long autobiographical poem has this title

explanation.surface: The opening to an important piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's best-known long poem has this title, so the second reading points to a specific work.
explanation.definitionFit: An opening movement leads into a larger piece, and Wordsworth's celebrated autobiographical poem bears the title.

clue.text: Quietly shared out in a manner of speaking

parts.note: p, for piano, is the musical direction meaning quietly

indicators.note: out means the letters of shared are put into disarray

explanation.surface: Something shared out softly, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' looks like a stock idiom, but it defines a word meaning put into words in a certain manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Expressed in particular words is to have been worded a certain way, a manner of speaking.

clue.text: Gives encouragement to sources of growth

definitions.meaning: the underground parts from which a plant grows

explanation.surface: Encouraging what makes things grow.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheer on a team is an idiom with this verb, and a plant's underground parts feed its growth.

clue.text: Where silver too can be unearthed in the Antipodes

definitions.text: Where silver too can be unearthed in the Antipodes

indicators.note: unearthed means the letters are dug up and turned over into a new order

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A place in Australasia where silver may also be mined.
explanation.walkthrough: AG, the chemical symbol for silver, and TOO are 'unearthed', scrambled; the region in New Zealand's South Island is famed for gold mining, so silver too fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago, in New Zealand's South Island, had a nineteenth-century gold rush, so precious metals have been dug there.

clue.text: Impenetrable and in a manner mean

parts.note: an air is a manner or bearing
tight means stingy, mean with money

explanation.surface: Someone who is both inscrutable and stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like a verb, but it is the adjective for stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sealed so nothing can pass through, like a sealed container, is to be impermeable.

clue.text: Exchanged Eire's currency in France

indicators.note: exchanged means the letters of the possessive are swapped about

parts.note: the letters of Eire's, with its s

explanation.surface: Irish money changed into French money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currency' is not money but something that flows, a current: the river Isère in south-east France.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is a current, and the Isère is a tributary of the Rhône in France.

clue.text: Drop out in a dig

indicators.note: out means the letters of drop are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Dropping out after a jibe.
explanation.definitionFit: A jab or poke, with the finger or elbow, is a dig.

clue.text: Not currently creditable due to some liability

definitions.text: Not currently creditable due to some liability

parts.words: Not currently creditable due to some liability
parts.note: someone behind with payments owes money still due, so they are not in credit

explanation.surface: An account not in credit because of a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: A person behind with payments still owes a sum that is due, so is not currently in credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Being late in paying a debt that is owed is the standard financial idiom for overdue amounts.

clue.text: Sweetheart with the right air

parts.note: the heart of sweet is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A loved one with just the right look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' is read as the heart of 'sweet', its middle letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: The ether is a poetic term for the upper air or clear sky.

clue.text: Time for reflection

indicators.note: for reflection means the word reads the same when mirrored, backwards as forwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A moment set aside for quiet thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflection' suggests thinking, but the word reads the same backwards, as in a mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is a time of day, twelve o'clock.

clue.text: To act so impetuously is anything but hair-raising

definitions.text: To act so impetuously is anything but hair-raising

parts.words: To act so impetuously is anything but hair-raising
parts.note: going at something in this way means rushing in recklessly, and having no hair is the opposite of hair-raising

explanation.surface: Rash action that is in no way frightening.
explanation.walkthrough: To go at something 'bald-headed' is an old idiom for charging in rashly; literally it means having no hair, so it cannot raise any.
explanation.definitionFit: Charging in without care is an old idiom based on hairlessness, the reverse of making hair stand up.
